deck.title: EHS Culture Measurement and Improvement Concept Cards

cards.backDefinition: The shared organizational values, priorities, expectations, and practices that shape how people understand and act on safety over time.
cards.whyItMatters: Culture influences what people treat as important when production pressure, uncertainty, or competing priorities make safety decisions less obvious.
cards.keyPoint: Culture is broader and more enduring than a single climate survey result.

sourceRefs.locator: Management Leadership > commitment from the top and continuous improvement

cards.backDefinition: Employees' shared perceptions of what the organization rewards, expects, values, and reinforces in the workplace with respect to safety.
cards.whyItMatters: Safety climate provides a measurable view of how workers currently experience safety priorities and can reveal weak signals before adverse outcomes occur.
cards.keyPoint: Climate is a measurable snapshot of shared safety perceptions.

cards.backDefinition: A structured evaluation of safety-climate factors using worker responses or other defined measures to identify strengths, maturity, and areas needing improvement.
cards.whyItMatters: Assessment converts perceptions into organized evidence that can be compared, discussed, prioritized, and revisited after interventions.
cards.keyPoint: Measure the same defined factors again after improvement actions to judge change.

sourceRefs.locator: S-CAT self-assessment, 37 items, 8 safety climate factors, tailored report

cards.backDefinition: Visible and sustained leadership action showing that safety and health are organizational priorities through decisions, resources, communication, and personal example.
cards.whyItMatters: Workers judge priorities from what leaders consistently do, so visible commitment strongly shapes whether safety expectations are trusted and followed.
cards.keyPoint: Commitment is demonstrated through actions, not policy statements alone.

sourceRefs.locator: Management Leadership > top management can demonstrate its commitment
Safety Climate Factors > Demonstrating management commitment

cards.backDefinition: The integration of safety into routine organizational priorities and decisions so it is treated as a persistent value rather than a temporary program objective.
cards.whyItMatters: When safety is integrated into planning and operational choices, workers receive a more consistent signal about how competing priorities should be resolved.
cards.keyPoint: A core value influences decisions even when no specific safety campaign is underway.

sourceRefs.locator: Safety Climate Factors > Aligning and integrating safety as a value
Management Leadership > factoring safety and health into operational planning and decisions

cards.backDefinition: Clear responsibility for safety expectations, decisions, actions, and follow-through at appropriate levels of the organization.
cards.whyItMatters: Accountability helps turn stated safety values into dependable behavior by making expectations and ownership visible instead of diffuse.
cards.keyPoint: Accountability should apply across organizational levels rather than being assigned only to safety staff.

sourceRefs.locator: Safety Climate Factors > Ensuring accountability at all levels

cards.backDefinition: Meaningful worker involvement in establishing, operating, evaluating, and improving safety and health activities, including reporting hazards and developing solutions.
cards.whyItMatters: Workers often have direct knowledge of task hazards and system weaknesses, and their involvement improves hazard recognition, ownership, trust, and program sustainability.
cards.keyPoint: Participation requires genuine opportunities, information, resources, and protection from retaliation.

sourceRefs.locator: Worker Participation > workers involved in establishing, operating, evaluating, and improving the program
Safety Climate Factors > Empowering and involving workers

cards.backDefinition: The timely two-way exchange of safety information, concerns, expectations, feedback, and management responses across levels of the organization.
cards.whyItMatters: Open communication helps workers raise hazards and learn what action followed, while leaders gain information needed to correct weak conditions and build trust.
cards.keyPoint: Communication is strongest when reporting is followed by visible feedback and action.

sourceRefs.locator: Action item 2 > report concerns and report back to workers about action taken

cards.backDefinition: The use of reports, evaluations, worker knowledge, and feedback to change organizational systems, practices, or controls and improve future safety performance.
cards.whyItMatters: Learning prevents the organization from repeatedly collecting safety information without converting it into better decisions, controls, and work practices.
cards.keyPoint: Information becomes organizational learning only when it drives effective change and is retained in practice.

sourceRefs.locator: Correct program shortcomings and identify opportunities to improve
Action item 4 > evaluate program performance and identify ways to improve it

cards.backDefinition: A repeatable process of assessing culture or climate, identifying weak factors, selecting interventions, implementing changes, and reassessing to evaluate improvement.
cards.whyItMatters: A cycle prevents culture work from ending with a survey score and links measurement to prioritized interventions and evidence of whether those interventions worked.
cards.keyPoint: Assess, prioritize, intervene, reassess, and refine.

sourceRefs.locator: Tailored report, intervention ideas, and retake S-CAT to evaluate effectiveness
Program evaluation and improvement > correct shortcomings and identify opportunities to improve
